*** Add File: /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s001/discovery/pilot1-20261005/1_7/terra/list.tsv
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.107.4	lost road with no city	The commentary contrasts aimless disappearance with a road that reaches a known end; Ps 107 first portrays desert wanderers unable to find a road to an inhabited city, a concrete scene of the former condition.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.107.7	straight road to a destination	After the city-less wandering of Ps 107, God leads the travelers by a straight way to a settled city; this gives the commentary's purposeful, destination-bearing sirat a close journey scene.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.23.3	shepherd leading paths of righteousness	The commentary's road is recognized through a guide and a flock rather than as a bare line; Ps 23 has the divine shepherd restore the traveler and lead him in right paths.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.119.176	lost sheep sought by its master	The final word dalin is heard beside an animal separated from its owner; the psalmist calls himself a lost sheep and asks God to seek him, joining straying to a continuing master-servant relation.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Jer.50.6	lost sheep misled by shepherds	Jeremiah calls Israel lost sheep whose shepherds made them wander from mountain to hill and forget their resting place; it directly joins the commentary's bad leader, lost flock, and missed destination.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.34.6	scattered flock with no seeker	The ownerless camel image is answered by Ezekiel's sheep scattered over mountains and hills while no one searches for them; the verse makes abandonment by responsible guides part of the straying scene.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.34.16	seeking and restoring the strayed	Where the commentary leaves open that the stray can cease being lost, God promises to seek the lost sheep and bring back the one driven away; the owner actively reverses dispersion.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Num.27.17	leader before a flock	Moses asks for a leader who goes out before and comes in before the community so that Israel will not be sheep without a shepherd; this closely matches the commentary's forward guide and people identified by the road they follow.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.13.21	visible guidance on the way	The commentary treats sirat as an ordinary journey with signs rather than a postmortem bridge; the pillar of cloud and fire goes before Israel to lead its actual day-and-night route.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.23.20	guardian on the road to a prepared place	God's messenger guards Israel on the way and brings it to a prepared destination, furnishing a precise counterpart to the commentary's guided road whose goodness comes from where it leads.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.8.2	wilderness guidance tests the heart	The commentary resists treating favor as an inherited status; Deuteronomy recalls that God led Israel through the wilderness in order to humble and test what was in its heart.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.8.16	manna as benefit and testing	The text's provision of manna is said to humble, test, and finally do Israel good; it supplies a close scriptural instance of a bestowed benefit that neither ends moral testing nor guarantees a fixed condition.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.30.16	walking as the condition of blessing	The commentary makes the way belong to those who actually walk it; Deuteronomy couples loving God, walking in his ways, and keeping commands with life, increase, and divine blessing.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.18.19	Abraham's household keeps the Lord's way	The commentary distinguishes descent from walking as earlier recipients walked; Abraham's descendants receive the promised outcome through being instructed to keep the Lord's way by righteousness and justice.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Judg.2.10	a later generation does not know the deeds	The commentary's procession of guided prophets is followed by descendants who can abandon their way; Judges explicitly introduces a subsequent generation that did not know the Lord or the work done for Israel.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.18.20	responsibility is not inherited	The commentary says the road is not inherited merely through descent. Ezekiel states that child and parent do not bear one another's guilt, making moral standing personal rather than genealogical.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Jer.6.16	ancient paths requested and refused	Jeremiah tells the people to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it, but records their refusal; it closely matches the commentary's prior walkers as a real but uncoercive guide.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Prov.13.20	companions determine a walker's outcome	The commentary makes good and bad fellow-travelers decisive. Proverbs says one who walks with the wise becomes wise, while a companion of fools suffers harm.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.119.105	lamp for feet and light for a path	The commentary develops road signs and walking feet; the psalm gives God's word the specific job of a lamp for the foot and a light for the path.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Isa.30.21	a voice identifies the road at each turn	The commentary's straight road is a route that must be recognized while walking. Isaiah pictures a word heard behind the traveler saying, "This is the way; walk in it," when turning right or left.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Jer.31.9	water and a level road for the returning community	The commentary joins guided travel, water, and a destination. Jeremiah's restoration oracle leads the weeping returnees by streams of water on an even path where they will not stumble.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Isa.49.10	compassion guiding a flock to springs	The page's shade, water, and flock imagery converges in Isaiah: the compassionate one leads the returned people and guides them by springs of water.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.95.10	people who err and do not know God's ways	The commentary separates active straying from an externally received condition. Ps 95 describes a people who go astray in their heart and do not know God's ways, locating the deviation in their own stance.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.95.11	wrath and failure to enter rest	The commentary makes wrath and being lost related yet distinct dangers with different ends. Ps 95 has divine wrath bar this erring people from God's rest, making the destination of the negative path explicit.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.32.8	turning aside from the commanded way for the calf	The commentary itself uses the calf episode to show a favored community turning aside. Exodus describes the same community as quickly turning from the commanded way in making the calf.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.32.10	wrath after the calf	The passive maghdub formula is illuminated by the narrative in which divine anger burns against the calf-making people; the source makes the wrath's historical trigger explicit without collapsing it into mere ethnic identity.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.32.14	intercession and relenting from announced disaster	The commentary calls wrath an threshold rather than a sealed door. In the calf narrative God relents from the disaster announced against the people after Moses's intercession.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Jer.18.8	a people turns and the announced judgment changes	The commentary connects the gayr/change language to a condition that can move from favor to wrath and back. Jeremiah explicitly says that if the warned nation turns from evil, God relents from the disaster planned for it.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.18.21	the wicked person turns and lives	The page's repentance sequence after anger is not merely communal: Ezekiel says that a wicked person who turns from sins and keeps the statutes will live, giving the stray a concrete route of return.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.36.26	stone heart replaced by flesh heart	The commentary contrasts the hard, shield-like texture beside wrath with softening beside favor. Ezekiel's replacement of a heart of stone by a heart of flesh makes that material contrast an explicit transformation.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.36.27	inner renewal causes walking in statutes	The commentary links softened interior life to a traversed way. Ezekiel follows the new heart with God's Spirit causing the people to walk in God's statutes, tying transformation directly to a manner of walking.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.22.1	returning a brother's strayed animal	The commentary's dalin carries a stray camel separated from its owner. Deuteronomy legislates the opposite response: do not ignore a brother's ox or sheep that has gone astray, but return it.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.22.2	caring for an animal when its owner is unknown	The definition of the lost camel stresses that its owner is not known. Deuteronomy imagines precisely that case and requires keeping the animal until its owner seeks it, so apparent ownerlessness is not final abandonment.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Mal.2.8	religious guides cause many to stumble	The commentary warns that the track one follows may belong to a misguiding companion. Malachi accuses priests of departing from the way and causing many to stumble by their instruction.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Isa.53.6	sheep each turning to its own way	The text hears dalin as both loss of a route and a dispersed flock. Isaiah describes all as sheep gone astray, each turning to its own way, giving the self-directed aspect of straying a flock image.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.37.12	graves opened and bodies brought up	The commentary pairs a body disappearing into earth with the claim that disappearance need not be annihilation. Ezekiel's vision has God open graves and bring the buried people up from them.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Dan.12.2	dust sleepers awakened to divergent ends	The page distinguishes vanishing into earth from a journey with an end. Daniel says that sleepers in the dust awake, with opposed eschatological outcomes, providing a Hebrew Bible answer to the question of the body lost in soil.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Isa.63.10	rebellion changes benefactor into enemy	The commentary follows a community from blessing to wrath when its inner condition changes. Isaiah recalls that the people rebelled and grieved God's spirit, so that their former helper turned to be their enemy.
+strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Deut.9.4	election is not proof of the recipient's righteousness	The commentary refuses to make the recipients of favor a permanently righteous lineage. Deuteronomy warns Israel not to explain its gift of land by saying it receives it because of its own righteousness.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Phil.3.17	walkers who embody an example	The commentary defines the requested route through people already on it. Paul tells readers to imitate him and to observe those who walk according to the example they have received, an unusually close formulation of a path recognized by walkers.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:1Pet.2.21	following another's footsteps	The trace left by earlier guided people is central to the commentary. First Peter says that Christ left an example so that believers should follow in his footsteps, making the image literal and ethical.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Rom.4.12	Abrahamic descent defined by walking in faith	The commentary says Abrahamic relation comes through walking as the earlier recipient walked. Paul calls Abraham father of those who do not merely possess a mark of descent but walk in the footsteps of his faith.

strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.107.4	lost road with no city	The commentary contrasts aimless disappearance with a road that reaches a known end; Ps 107 first portrays desert wanderers unable to find a road to an inhabited city, a concrete scene of the former condition.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.107.7	straight road to a destination	After the city-less wandering of Ps 107, God leads the travelers by a straight way to a settled city; this gives the commentary's purposeful, destination-bearing sirat a close journey scene.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.23.3	shepherd leading paths of righteousness	The commentary's road is recognized through a guide and a flock rather than as a bare line; Ps 23 has the divine shepherd restore the traveler and lead him in right paths.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.119.176	lost sheep sought by its master	The final word dalin is heard beside an animal separated from its owner; the psalmist calls himself a lost sheep and asks God to seek him, joining straying to a continuing master-servant relation.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Jer.50.6	lost sheep misled by shepherds	Jeremiah calls Israel lost sheep whose shepherds made them wander from mountain to hill and forget their resting place; it directly joins the commentary's bad leader, lost flock, and missed destination.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.34.6	scattered flock with no seeker	The ownerless camel image is answered by Ezekiel's sheep scattered over mountains and hills while no one searches for them; the verse makes abandonment by responsible guides part of the straying scene.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.34.16	seeking and restoring the strayed	Where the commentary leaves open that the stray can cease being lost, God promises to seek the lost sheep and bring back the one driven away; the owner actively reverses dispersion.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Num.27.17	leader before a flock	Moses asks for a leader who goes out before and comes in before the community so that Israel will not be sheep without a shepherd; this closely matches the commentary's forward guide and people identified by the road they follow.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.13.21	visible guidance on the way	The commentary treats sirat as an ordinary journey with signs rather than a postmortem bridge; the pillar of cloud and fire goes before Israel to lead its actual day-and-night route.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Exod.23.20	guardian on the road to a prepared place	God's messenger guards Israel on the way and brings it to a prepared destination, furnishing a precise counterpart to the commentary's guided road whose goodness comes from where it leads.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.8.2	wilderness guidance tests the heart	The commentary resists treating favor as an inherited status; Deuteronomy recalls that God led Israel through the wilderness in order to humble and test what was in its heart.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.8.16	manna as benefit and testing	The text's provision of manna is said to humble, test, and finally do Israel good; it supplies a close scriptural instance of a bestowed benefit that neither ends moral testing nor guarantees a fixed condition.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.30.16	walking as the condition of blessing	The commentary makes the way belong to those who actually walk it; Deuteronomy couples loving God, walking in his ways, and keeping commands with life, increase, and divine blessing.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.18.19	Abraham's household keeps the Lord's way	The commentary distinguishes descent from walking as earlier recipients walked; Abraham's descendants receive the promised outcome through being instructed to keep the Lord's way by righteousness and justice.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Judg.2.10	a later generation does not know the deeds	The commentary's procession of guided prophets is followed by descendants who can abandon their way; Judges explicitly introduces a subsequent generation that did not know the Lord or the work done for Israel.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ezek.18.20	responsibility is not inherited	The commentary says the road is not inherited merely through descent. Ezekiel states that child and parent do not bear one another's guilt, making moral standing personal rather than genealogical.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Jer.6.16	ancient paths requested and refused	Jeremiah tells the people to ask for the ancient paths, find the good way, and walk in it, but records their refusal; it closely matches the commentary's prior walkers as a real but uncoercive guide.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Prov.13.20	companions determine a walker's outcome	The commentary makes good and bad fellow-travelers decisive. Proverbs says one who walks with the wise becomes wise, while a companion of fools suffers harm.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.119.105	lamp for feet and light for a path	The commentary develops road signs and walking feet; the psalm gives God's word the specific job of a lamp for the foot and a light for the path.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Isa.30.21	a voice identifies the road at each turn	The commentary's straight road is a route that must be recognized while walking. Isaiah pictures a word heard behind the traveler saying, "This is the way; walk in it," when turning right or left.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Jer.31.9	water and a level road for the returning community	The commentary joins guided travel, water, and a destination. Jeremiah's restoration oracle leads the weeping returnees by streams of water on an even path where they will not stumble.

+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Isa.55.7	forsaking a way and returning for mercy	The commentary makes the lost condition recoverable through a change of walking and repentance. Isaiah commands the wicked to forsake their way and return to the Lord, whose mercy and pardon answer that turn.
+strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Jer.7.24	walking in stubborn counsel and going backward	The commentary contrasts the forward trace of guided people with following one's own desire or misleading predecessors. +medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.30.3	return and gathering after dispersion	The commentary sets a united company on one route against dispersal from it. Deuteronomy describes God restoring the fortunes of a returning people and gathering them from the peoples among whom they have been scattered.
+medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Num.20.8	water for a congregation and its livestock	The commentary's journey imagery joins a guide, water, and a flock or herd. +medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.1.1	walking in wicked counsel	The commentary warns that a track may be defined by the wrong companions and ancestors. Ps 1 locates the blessed person's first refusal in not walking in the counsel of the wicked, before its standing and sitting images of belonging.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Luke.1.79	guiding feet into the way of peace	The commentary repeatedly locates guidance in actual feet and a road rather than an abstract orientation. Zechariah's hymn asks for light that will guide human feet into the way of peace.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:John.12.35	walking in darkness without knowing one's destination	The commentary distinguishes a traveler carried toward a destination from one who has lost direction. Jesus warns that the person who walks in darkness does not know where he is going, a sharply corresponding formulation.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Matt.15.14	blind guides and a shared fall	The commentary makes the identity of the guide decisive and notices sight as necessary for finding the route. Jesus calls the Pharisees blind guides; when blind lead blind, both fall into a pit.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:John.10.5	sheep refuse an unknown voice	The page's flock is safe only when it knows its guide rather than following every track. In the continuation of the shepherd image, sheep flee rather than follow a stranger because they do not know that voice.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Rom.11.20	former branches broken off and present standing by faith	The commentary argues that a community can pass from favor into judgment rather than carrying favor as descent. +strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.36	seed must die before it comes to life	The commentary's two forms of disappearance ask whether entry into earth means extinction or a directed transformation. +strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.33	bad company corrupts good character	The commentary's bad companion can divert a traveler after guidance has been received. Paul makes the same social mechanism explicit by warning that bad associations corrupt good character.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:2Pet.2.15	forsaking the straight way and following Balaam	The commentary joins departure from a straight track to imitation of a misleading predecessor. Second Peter says false teachers have forsaken the straight way, gone astray, and followed Balaam's way.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Heb.12.13	straight paths for feet that heal the lame	The commentary's road is not merely a verdict but a route that can steady or lose a walker. Hebrews asks the community to make straight paths for its feet so that what is lame is healed rather than dislocated.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 2:9	cling to a good way and avoid an evil one	The commentary examines right paths, false companions, and distinct negative routes. +medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Avot 1:7	distance from a bad neighbor and the wicked	The commentary's companion may either sustain the route or lead one away from it. Avot instructs its reader to keep far from a bad neighbor and not join the wicked, a rabbinic social safeguard for the path.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Babylonian Talmud, Makkot 10b	one is led in the way one chooses	The commentary differentiates God's bestowal of guidance from the traveler's active straying. Makkot crystallizes that tension in its maxim that a person is led along the way that person wants to go.
+medium	tevrat	paralel	Tobit 4:19	prayer that ways be made straight	Tobit's fatherly instruction combines fidelity, wise counsel, and a prayer that the son's ways be made straight and his paths prosper. It is a Jewish family-to-traveler counterpart to the commentary's route that must be walked rather than merely inherited.
*** End Patch";
